concepts.name: The first law of thermodynamics, $\kdEint = \kQh - \kW$
concepts.statement: The first law is the law of conservation of energy stated in the form most useful when heat transfer and doing work are the ways energy enters and leaves a system. The change in internal energy of a system equals the net heat transfer into the system minus the net work done by the system, so that positive heat transfer adds energy to the system and positive work takes energy from it, and whatever comes in and is not spent as work is stored as internal energy.

concepts.name: Sign conventions for heat transfer and work
concepts.statement: In the first law, heat transfer is positive when it is into the system and work is positive when it is done by the system. The convention matters because the same physical event, heat leaving a body or work being done on it, enters the equation with a minus sign, and a reader who mixes the two conventions will find the internal energy going the wrong way. Some texts define work against the external pressure and so write the law with a plus sign; this book does not.

concepts.name: Heat transfer and work are both energy in transit
concepts.statement: Heat transfer and doing work are the two everyday means of bringing energy into or taking energy out of a system, and they are different processes: heat transfer is driven by a temperature difference and is disorganized, while work is a macroscopic force exerted through a distance and is organized. Yet both can produce the same result, a warmer tire whether the Sun heated it or the pump compressed it, and once the temperature has risen there is no telling which did it. Neither is stored as such in a system; both change the internal energy, which is a different kind of thing.

concepts.name: Internal energy $\kEint$
concepts.statement: The internal energy of a system is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its atoms and molecules, which is to say the sum of their mechanical energy. Because no one can keep track of every atom, the section deals with averages and distributions and, macroscopically, with a few quantities such as pressure, volume and temperature that the internal energy turns out to depend on. It is the account that heat transfer and work pay into and draw from.

concepts.name: The change in internal energy is independent of path, $\kdEint = \kEinttwo - \kEintone$
concepts.statement: Experiment shows that the internal energy of a system depends only on the state of the system and not on how it reached that state. The change in internal energy between State 1 and State 2 is therefore the same for every path between them, while the heat transfer and the work done each depend on the path taken. This is what makes internal energy easier to work with than either heat or work: if the state is known, the change in internal energy follows from a few macroscopic variables.

concepts.name: Find the change in internal energy from the net heat transfer and the net work
concepts.statement: A problem gives heat transfer into and out of a system and work done on and by it; the net heat transfer is heat in minus heat out, the net work is work by minus work on, and the first law gives the change in internal energy. The same procedure, run the other way, finds an unknown heat transfer from a known change in internal energy and a known work, which is how the section's problems about the human body are solved.

concepts.name: Human metabolism and the first law
concepts.statement: Human metabolism is the conversion of food into heat transfer, work and stored fat. Taking the body as the system, heat transfer to the surroundings makes Q negative and the work the body does on the world makes W positive, so the body loses internal energy and food, which enters as chemical potential energy and may be counted as work done on the body, replaces it. Eating too much makes the change in internal energy positive and the surplus is stored as fat; eating too little makes it negative and the body metabolizes its own fat. The body also shows that many thermodynamic processes are irreversible, since fat can be turned into work and heat but work and heat cannot be turned back into fat.

concepts.name: Heat engine
concepts.statement: A heat engine is a machine that uses heat transfer to do work. Car engines and steam turbines are examples. Heat transfer into a gas in a cylinder raises its pressure, the gas pushes a piston through a distance and so does work on the outside world, and to repeat the process heat must leave the gas so that its pressure falls and the piston can be returned. The first law governs every step of it, and the section's simple processes are the pieces every heat engine is built from.

concepts.name: Work done at constant pressure, $\kW = \kPr\Delta V$
concepts.statement: A process in which a gas does work on a piston at constant pressure is an isobaric process. The force on the piston is the pressure times the piston's area, the work is that force times the distance the piston moves, and the area times the distance is the change in volume, so the work done is the pressure times the change in volume. A positive change in volume means work done by the gas on the outside world. Pressure is an energy per unit volume, as the fluids chapters noted, and here some of that energy becomes work.

concepts.name: Work is the area under the curve on a $PV$ diagram
concepts.statement: A graph of pressure against volume shows a process as a path, and the work done on or by a system in going from one state to another is the area under that path. For a constant pressure the area is a rectangle, the pressure times the change in volume; for a pressure that varies, the area is approximated by strips each of average pressure times its small change in volume and the total work is their sum. A path walked toward smaller volume has a negative area, which is work done on the system.

concepts.name: The work done depends on the path taken, not only on the endpoints
concepts.statement: Two paths between the same two states on a PV diagram enclose different areas, so the work done along them differs, and more work is done along the path that runs at higher pressure. This is the path dependence that the first law's Q and W both have and that the internal energy does not, made visible: the endpoints fix the change in internal energy, and the path fixes how much of it arrives as work.

concepts.name: Isochoric process, $\kW = 0$
concepts.statement: A process at constant volume is isochoric. The volume does not change, so the gas moves no piston and no work is done, and any heat transfer goes entirely into the internal energy. On a PV diagram an isochoric process is a vertical path, and it encloses no area.

concepts.name: The net work of a cyclical process is the area inside its loop on a $PV$ diagram
concepts.statement: A cyclical process returns the system to its starting point, and its net work is the area inside the closed loop it forms on a PV diagram, because the positive area under the outward legs and the negative area under the return legs leave only the interior. The loop must be traversed clockwise for the net work to be positive, that is, for the engine to put work out; traversed counterclockwise, the same loop takes work in. The area is often easier to compute than the work along each leg, and comparing the areas of different loops shows which process produces the most work.

concepts.name: Isothermal process of an ideal gas, $\kQh = \kW$
concepts.statement: An isothermal process is one at constant temperature. For an ideal gas, PV is then constant, and because the internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas depends on temperature alone it does not change, so the net heat transfer into the gas must equal the net work done by the gas: just enough heat comes in to replace the work done. An isothermal process is inherently slow, since heat must flow continuously and spread through the gas so that no region is hotter than another.

concepts.name: Adiabatic process, $\kQh = 0$ and $\kdEint = -\kW$
concepts.statement: An adiabatic process is one in which no heat transfer takes place, achieved by very effective insulation or by running the process so fast that heat has no time to flow. Because Q is zero, the work the gas does comes entirely from its internal energy, so the temperature falls during an adiabatic expansion and the pressure with it. The adiabatic path from a point therefore lies below the isothermal path from the same point, and less work is done along it.

concepts.name: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas, $\kEint = \tfrac{3}{2}Nk\kTemp$
concepts.statement: The average kinetic energy of an atom in a monatomic ideal gas is three halves of Boltzmann's constant times the absolute temperature, and kinetic energy is the only internal energy such a gas has, so its total internal energy is N times that average. The internal energy of an ideal gas therefore depends on its temperature alone, which is what makes the isothermal and adiabatic arguments work. Diatomic gases such as air have different formulas.

concepts.name: Reversible process
concepts.statement: A reversible process is one in which both the system and its environment can return to exactly the states they were in by following the reverse path. Isothermal and adiabatic processes are reversible in principle, but real macroscopic processes never are, because any dissipative mechanism such as friction or turbulence produces heat transfer to the environment in both directions of the piston's travel, and reversibility would require the direction of heat transfer to reverse. That real processes cannot be reversed points to a second law of thermodynamics, which the following sections state.

concepts.name: Isobaric process
concepts.statement: An isobaric process is one that takes place at constant pressure, as when a gas expands against a piston that keeps its pressure fixed.

concepts.name: Irreversible process
concepts.statement: An irreversible process is one that depends on path: it goes in one direction only under a given set of conditions, and the reverse path differs fundamentally. Heat transfer from hot to cold, the conversion of kinetic energy to heat by friction and the spread of a puff of gas through a vacuum chamber are all one-way, and none of them violates the first law, so some other law must forbid their reverse. That law is the second law of thermodynamics.

concepts.name: The second law of thermodynamics, first expression: heat transfer occurs spontaneously from hotter to colder bodies and never spontaneously in the reverse direction
concepts.statement: The familiar direction of heat transfer is the first form of the second law. Heat transfer occurs spontaneously from higher- to lower-temperature bodies but never spontaneously in the reverse direction; put another way, no process can have as its sole result heat transfer from a cooler to a hotter object. A cold object in contact with a hot one never gets colder.

concepts.name: The second law of thermodynamics, second expression: no cyclical process can convert heat transfer from a reservoir completely to work
concepts.statement: It is impossible in any system for heat transfer from a reservoir to convert completely to work in a cyclical process in which the system returns to its initial state. Every heat engine must therefore reject some heat to a cold reservoir; the wish that the work output equal the heat input, with nothing lost to the environment, cannot be granted. This is the form of the second law that limits the efficiency of every engine.

concepts.name: Cyclical process
concepts.statement: A cyclical process brings a system, such as the gas in a cylinder, back to its original state at the end of every cycle. Most heat engines, reciprocating pistons and turbines alike, use cyclical processes. Because the internal energy depends only on the state, it is the same at the start and end of every cycle, so its change over a cycle is zero and the first law reduces to the statement that the net work done equals the net heat transfer.

concepts.name: Work output of a heat engine, $\kW = \kQH - \kQC$
concepts.statement: Over a complete cycle the internal energy of the engine does not change, so the net work done by the engine equals the net heat transfer into it, which is the heat transfer from the hot reservoir minus the heat transfer into the cold reservoir. The trouble with every engine is that the heat transfer to the cold reservoir is never zero and is usually large.

concepts.name: Efficiency of a heat engine, $\text{Eff} = \kW/\kQH = 1 - \kQC/\kQH$
concepts.statement: The conversion efficiency is the ratio of what we get to what we spend: for a heat engine, the net work output divided by the heat transfer into the engine. Since the work is the difference of the two heat transfers, the efficiency is also one minus the ratio of the heat transfer to the cold reservoir to the heat transfer from the hot one, which shows that an efficiency of one would need no heat transfer to the environment at all. All the Q's are positive, with direction shown by sign or on the schematic.

concepts.name: Find an engine's work, waste heat or efficiency from the other two
concepts.statement: Given any two of the heat transfer into an engine, the heat transfer to the environment and the work output, the cycle's energy balance gives the third, and the efficiency follows as work over heat in. Run the other way, a stated efficiency and a heat input give the work and the waste heat. A large power station is a heat engine, so the same arithmetic gives its daily output, its efficiency and, with the fuel's energy content, the fuel it burns and the carbon dioxide it releases.

concepts.name: The Otto cycle
concepts.statement: The Otto cycle is the thermodynamic cycle of the four-stroke gasoline engine, two adiabatic processes and two isochoric ones. An adiabatic compression corresponds to the compression stroke, heat transfer in at constant volume to the burning of the fuel, an adiabatic expansion to the power stroke, and heat transfer out at constant volume to the exhaust and intake. The work out along the expansion exceeds the work in along the compression because the pressure is higher, so there is a net work output, and the cooler the compression and the hotter the expansion the larger the loop and the more efficient the engine, which points to the reservoir temperatures as what sets the limit.

concepts.name: The second law of thermodynamics
concepts.statement: The second law of thermodynamics states that heat transfer occurs spontaneously only from a hotter body to a colder one, never the reverse, and that no cyclical process can convert heat transfer from a reservoir completely into work. The chapter gives it in several equivalent forms.

concepts.name: The Carnot cycle and the Carnot engine
concepts.statement: Sadi Carnot devised in 1824 a theoretical cycle that is the most efficient cyclical process possible, made of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes, all of them reversible. Any heat engine that uses it is a Carnot engine. What defines the cycle is that only reversible processes are used, since irreversible processes involve dissipative factors such as friction and turbulence that increase the heat transfer to the environment and lower the efficiency. The ideal Carnot engine has zero power, like the drinking bird, which is why it is a limit and not a design.

concepts.name: The second law of thermodynamics, third expression: a Carnot engine has the greatest possible efficiency between two given temperatures
concepts.statement: Stated in terms of reversible processes, the second law has a third form: a Carnot engine operating between two given temperatures has the greatest possible efficiency of any heat engine operating between them, and all engines employing only reversible processes have this same maximum efficiency between the same temperatures. What Carnot discovered in his study of steam engines was this law.

concepts.name: Carnot efficiency, $\text{Eff}_{\text{C}} = 1 - \kTempc/\kTemph$
concepts.statement: For a perfect heat engine the ratio of the heat transfer to the cold reservoir to the heat transfer from the hot one equals the ratio of the absolute temperatures of the two reservoirs, so the maximum efficiency is one minus the cold temperature over the hot, both in kelvins. An efficiency of 100% would need a cold reservoir at absolute zero, which is impossible in practice and in theory, and the greatest efficiencies come from the hottest possible hot reservoir and the coldest possible cold one. No real engine reaches the Carnot efficiency.

concepts.name: Find a maximum efficiency, or a reservoir temperature, from the two reservoir temperatures
concepts.statement: The reservoir temperatures are converted to kelvins and the Carnot efficiency follows; or a stated efficiency and one reservoir temperature give the other. A real engine reaching some fraction of the maximum is handled the same way, and two engines run in series, the second on the exhaust of the first, have an overall Carnot efficiency equal to that of one engine between the outer temperatures.

concepts.name: Real engines fall short of the Carnot efficiency
concepts.statement: All real processes are irreversible, so no real engine is as efficient as a Carnot engine between the same reservoirs; a nuclear station's 35% is a little better than 0.7 of its maximum, and coal, oil and gas stations reach about 42% because their boilers run hotter. Even the best engine has dissipative processes in its peripheral equipment, such as transformers and transmissions, which convert some of the work output back into heat transfer to the environment and lower the overall efficiency further.

concepts.name: Carnot engine
concepts.statement: A Carnot engine is a heat engine that runs on the Carnot cycle, using only reversible processes.

concepts.name: Heat pump, $\kQH = \kQC + \kW$
concepts.statement: Heat pumps, air conditioners and refrigerators move heat transfer from cold to hot. They are heat engines run backward: heat transfer occurs from a cold reservoir and into a hot one, and this requires a work input, which is itself converted to heat transfer, so the heat transfer to the hot reservoir is the heat from the cold reservoir plus the work. A heat pump's mission is the heat delivered to a warm space; a refrigerator's or an air conditioner's is the heat removed from a cold one. The reader pays only for the work and gets the heat from the cold outdoors at no cost.

concepts.name: The four components of a heat pump
concepts.statement: A heat pump has a condenser, an expansion valve, an evaporator and a compressor, joined in a loop that a working fluid runs round. In the outdoor evaporator the fluid takes heat from the cold air and becomes a gas; the electrically driven compressor raises its temperature and pressure and forces it into the indoor condenser coils, where, being hotter than the room, it gives up heat and condenses; the liquid then passes back through the expansion valve and cools as it expands. In a cooling cycle the two coils exchange roles and the fluid runs the other way.

concepts.name: Coefficient of performance of a heat pump, $\text{COP}_{\text{hp}} = \kQH/\kW$
concepts.statement: A heat pump is judged by how much heat transfer it delivers to the warm space compared with the work it takes, so its coefficient of performance is the heat transfer to the hot reservoir divided by the work input. Since a heat engine's efficiency is the work over that same heat transfer, the coefficient of performance is the reciprocal of the efficiency, and because every efficiency is less than one the coefficient is always greater than one: a heat pump always delivers more heat than the work put into it.

concepts.name: Heat pumps work best when the temperature difference is small
concepts.statement: Because the coefficient of performance is the reciprocal of the efficiency and the Carnot efficiency shrinks as the two reservoir temperatures approach one another, a heat pump does best when the difference between outdoors and indoors is small and worst in very cold climates. Friction and other irreversible processes do not help a heat pump as they lower an engine's efficiency; they take part of the work input as heat before it reaches the pump and lower the coefficient of performance. Real heat pumps reach values from about 2 to 4, and they are most economical where winters are mild and summers warm.

concepts.name: Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator or air conditioner, $\text{COP}_{\text{ref}} = \kQC/\kW = \text{COP}_{\text{hp}} - 1$
concepts.statement: An air conditioner or refrigerator is judged by how much heat transfer it removes from the cold environment compared with the work input, so its coefficient of performance is the heat transfer from the cold reservoir divided by the work. What a heat pump counts as its benefit a refrigerator counts as waste heat. Because the heat to the hot reservoir is the heat from the cold one plus the work, the refrigerator's coefficient is the heat pump's minus one for the same engine between the same temperatures, and real refrigerators reach values from 2 to 6 because their temperature differences are small.

concepts.name: Find the best coefficient of performance from the two reservoir temperatures
concepts.statement: A Carnot engine reversed gives the best possible heat pump or refrigerator, so the best coefficient of performance follows from the Carnot efficiency between the two reservoir temperatures in kelvins: the reciprocal for a heat pump, and one less than that for a refrigerator. With a work input given, the heat delivered or removed follows, and with a price per kilowatt-hour so does the cost, which is how the section compares a heat pump with burning natural gas.

concepts.name: The energy efficiency rating
concepts.statement: The energy efficiency rating is a coefficient of performance in mixed units, the British thermal units of heat transfer from the cold environment per hour divided by the watts of power input, still used for room air conditioners in several countries. Room units come with ratings from 6 to 12, and though the rating is not the same as the coefficient of performance it serves for comparison: the greater the rating, the cheaper the unit is to run and the more it is likely to cost to buy.

concepts.name: Work a problem through the problem-solving strategy for thermodynamics
concepts.statement: The book's strategy has seven steps: decide whether heat, work or internal energy is involved; identify the system and draw a labeled diagram of the energy flow; list the unknowns, remembering that a maximum efficiency means a Carnot engine and that efficiency is not the same as coefficient of performance; list the knowns, distinguishing heat in from heat out and work in from work out and naming the kind of process; solve the appropriate equation; substitute with units; and check that the answer is reasonable, an efficiency below one and a coefficient of performance above one.

concepts.name: Entropy $\kSent$
concepts.statement: Entropy is a measure of a system's disorder and of the unavailability of its energy to do work. Although all forms of energy can be used to do work, it is not always possible, even in principle, to convert all of a system's energy into work, and entropy measures how much cannot be. Like internal energy it is a property of state: the entropy of a system depends only on its state and not on how it got there, which is what lets its change be computed for any process, real or imagined.

concepts.name: Change in entropy, $\kdS = (\kQh/\kTemp)_{\text{rev}}$
concepts.statement: The change in entropy of a system in a reversible process is the heat transfer, positive into the system and negative out of it, divided by the absolute temperature at which it takes place, in joules per kelvin. For a Carnot cycle the heat transfers at the two reservoirs are in the ratio of their absolute temperatures, so this ratio is the same at both. Where the temperature changes a little during the process, use the average temperature. The definition holds strictly for reversible processes, but because entropy is a property of state, you can find the change for any real process by imagining a reversible one between the same two states.

concepts.name: There is an increase in entropy for any system undergoing an irreversible process
concepts.statement: Spontaneous heat transfer from hot to cold is irreversible, and its total entropy change is found by imagining a reversible loss from the hot reservoir and a reversible gain by the cold one. Because the change in entropy is the heat over the temperature, the same heat makes a larger change at the lower temperature: the hot reservoir's loss is smaller than the cold reservoir's gain, and the total increases. The result is general: every irreversible process increases the entropy of the system.

concepts.name: The second law of thermodynamics stated in terms of entropy: the total entropy of a system either increases or remains constant in any process; it never decreases
concepts.statement: The total change in entropy over a Carnot cycle is the hot reservoir's loss plus the cold reservoir's gain, and because the two heat transfers are in the ratio of the temperatures the total is zero; this holds for any reversible process, which changes neither the entropy of the system nor that of its surroundings. Real processes are irreversible and increase the total entropy. So there are only two possibilities, and the fourth form of the second law says so: entropy is constant in a reversible process and increases in an irreversible one, and it never decreases. Heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot because entropy would decrease. Entropy, unlike energy, is not conserved.

concepts.name: Energy made unavailable by an increase in entropy, $\kWunavail = \kdS\cdot\kTempo$
concepts.statement: When entropy increases, a certain amount of energy becomes permanently unavailable to do work. The energy is not lost, but its character is changed, so that some of it can never again be converted into an organized force acting through a distance. The amount that becomes unavailable is the increase in entropy times the lowest temperature utilized. Two perfect engines fed the same heat give different work when one is fed after the heat has already fallen to a colder reservoir, and the difference is exactly this quantity.

concepts.name: The heat death of the universe
concepts.statement: As entropy increases, less and less of the energy in the universe is available to do work. Temperature differences, which are what heat engines run on, arose as the universe matured and are being used up; on Earth the stores of fuel and the differences in temperature that give wind, geothermal and tidal energy will be spent, and though the Sun replenishes some of them for another five billion years, in the very long run all stars will die and all temperatures will equalize. The universe is destined for thermodynamic equilibrium, maximum entropy, when no work can be done, though calculations suggest that is at least 10¹⁰⁰ years away.

concepts.name: Entropy is a measure of disorder
concepts.statement: Entropy is related not only to the unavailability of energy but to disorder, as Boltzmann first proposed. Melting a block of ice turns a structured arrangement of molecules into a liquid in which they have no fixed positions, and the entropy rises by a large amount. Mixing equal masses of warm and cool water produces three results at once: the entropy increases, some energy becomes unavailable to do work because there is no longer a temperature difference to run an engine on, and the single mass at one temperature is less orderly than two masses at two. These three results are essentially equivalent.

concepts.name: Local decreases in entropy, $\kdStot = \kdSsyst + \kdSenvir > 0$
concepts.statement: Living organisms are highly structured and much lower in entropy than what they grow from, and some take this to mean that evolution violates the second law. It does not: the entropy of one part of the universe can always decrease provided the total change is positive, so the system's change can be negative as long as the environment's is positive and larger in magnitude. Picking up scattered marbles or building a bridge lowers the entropy of those systems by energy transfer, and the Earth, intercepting a small part of the Sun's heat transfer into deep space, is a heat engine of high complexity that produces small local decreases in entropy at the cost of a large total increase.

concepts.name: Find an entropy change from a heat transfer and a temperature
concepts.statement: The heat transfer and the absolute temperature at which it takes place give the change in entropy; where the temperature changes a little, the average temperature in kelvins serves, and where the heat transfer is a phase change it is the mass times the latent heat. The total change for a transfer between two bodies is the sum of a negative change at the hotter temperature and a positive one at the colder, and the energy made unavailable follows by multiplying the total by the lowest temperature.

concepts.name: Macrostate and microstate
concepts.statement: A macrostate is an overall property of a system, such as the total number of heads and tails in a toss or the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas; it does not specify the details. A microstate is a detailed description of every element of the system, such as the order in which the heads and tails came up or the positions and velocities of every atom. Each macrostate can be reached by some number of microstates, and the analysis assumes that every microstate is equally probable, which requires the coins to be fair.

concepts.name: Disorder is vastly more likely than order
concepts.statement: The most orderly macrostates, all heads or all tails, have the fewest microstates and are the least likely; the most disorderly, an even split, have the most and are the most likely. With five coins the odds are 30 to 2 that a toss leaves an orderly array less orderly; with a hundred, there is one way to get all heads and 10²⁹ ways to get fifty, and a toss a second would produce all heads once in 2 × 10²² years, a trillion times the age of the universe. The growth in the odds favoring disorder continues as the system grows, so for the atoms of a gas the orderly macrostate, all in one corner, is so unlikely that it never happens.

concepts.name: Boltzmann's entropy, $\kSent = k\ln W$
concepts.statement: Boltzmann proved that the entropy of a system in a given macrostate is Boltzmann's constant times the natural logarithm of the number of microstates corresponding to that macrostate, and that this expression is equivalent to the definition of the change in entropy as heat transfer over temperature. Because the number of microstates is proportional to the probability of the macrostate, entropy is directly related to probability: the more likely the state, the greater its entropy. The second law then has its explanation at the most basic level, since a decrease in entropy is a move to a less probable state, and for a macroscopic system the odds against it are so long that it is never observed.

concepts.name: Find a change in entropy from counts of microstates, $\kdS = k\ln W_{\text{f}} - k\ln W_{\text{i}}$
concepts.statement: The change in entropy between two macrostates is Boltzmann's constant times the difference of the logarithms of their numbers of microstates, read from a table or counted. The ratio of the two numbers of microstates is how much more likely one macrostate is than the other, and it says whether a given decrease in entropy could ever be seen: a change of 10⁻²¹ J/K is a one in 10³⁰ chance, so a macroscopic decrease of the order of 10³ J/K is an utter impossibility.

concepts.name: The statistical explanation of the second law
concepts.statement: The several formulations of the second law say what happens; the statistical view says why. Heat transfer goes only from hot to cold, energy becomes ever less available and the universe grows more disorderly because disorder is vastly more probable than order, and a macroscopic system has so many atoms that the improbable never occurs. The gas that fills its container will never gather in one corner; with energy transfer from outside it could be forced there and its entropy lowered, but at the cost of a larger increase elsewhere, and left alone it disperses again. Entropy can decrease, but for any macroscopic system the outcome is so unlikely that it will never be observed.

concepts.name: Work a problem through the problem-solving strategy for entropy
concepts.statement: The book's strategy has seven steps: decide whether entropy is involved; identify the system and draw a labeled diagram of the energy flow; list the unknowns; list the knowns, identifying the heat transfer, the temperature at which it takes place and the initial and final states; solve the appropriate equation, remembering that the change in entropy between any two states can be found from a reversible process joining them; substitute with units; and check that the answer is reasonable, the total entropy increasing for any real process and disordered states being the more probable.

concepts.name: Macrostate
concepts.statement: A macrostate is an overall property of a system, such as the total number of heads and tails in a set of coin tosses, without regard to the order in which they arise.

concepts.name: Microstate
concepts.statement: A microstate is one detailed arrangement of a system, such as one particular sequence of heads and tails, and many microstates may belong to the same macrostate.

concepts.name: Statistical analysis
concepts.statement: Statistical analysis examines a system by counting its possibilities, such as the microstates that belong to each macrostate, to find how likely each outcome is.
